title: Right cash, right place
notes: Good morning, Alex. Good morning, Shreya. Thanks for making the time. Here’s the plan. I’ll show the problem and the live app, then we’ll cover readiness, risks, and next steps. Does that work? (pause) From our last conversation, we agreed on one business outcome: reduce the cash sitting idle and lower the cost of moving it, without increasing cash-outs. Alex, is that still the right outcome to anchor on today? (pause) Shreya, we also agreed that any solution has to pass two tests: it must protect sensitive data, and it has to be practical for your team to operate. Are those still the right technical priorities? (pause) Great. I’ll use those two outcomes as the lens for the demo. One quick note: everything you’ll see uses synthetic data.

title: Where we are today
notes: Let me start with the scope we agreed. Your cash operations cover 159 branches and 520 machines — 400 ATMs and 120 cash recyclers. They’re served by three cash centres and thirty armoured vans on a fixed five-day cycle. We’ve kept the MVP tighter: one region, Khon Kaen, and one daily decision — where should cash go tomorrow? The goal is less idle cash and fewer cash-outs without transforming the whole network at once.

title: What it costs today
notes: Here’s what the synthetic plan day looks like. About 1.56 billion baht is sitting in machines and vaults. Only fourteen point seven percent of stops land inside opening hours. Sixty-four machines are at cash-out risk. The fixed cycle drives 135 stops and 1,711 kilometres, when demand needs 97 stops. One assumption: at a two-percent cost of funds, releasing 43 million baht is worth roughly 0.9 million baht a year. The operating case doesn’t depend on that assumption.

title: Why now
notes: Alex, let me test the urgency with you. PromptPay and QR can make a fixed cycle overstock more each year, while New Year, Songkran, and payday still create sharp local demand. CIT and fuel costs are rising too. When does the current CIT contract renew? (pause) In this scenario, waiting adds about 125,000 baht a month in CIT cost. Which matters most right now: cost, cash-out risk, or the planning cycle? (pause) Got it. I’ll use that lens as we go.

title: Why it happens
notes: Shreya, the root cause isn’t one bad route. The ATM switch, cash-centre systems, CIT logs, core banking, and holiday spreadsheets all sit apart. Local knowledge, like a mall ATM opening late, stays in radio calls. Planning happens in Excel with day-old data and a calendar rule. There’s no forecast, feedback loop, clean override audit, or shared security model for custodian PII and depot access. The data, forecast, and people’s know-how never meet in one place.

title: The solution in four steps
notes: Shreya, let me show you what sits underneath. First, unify the feeds with Lakeflow pipelines and govern them in Unity Catalog. Next, predict machine demand through Model Serving. Then decide tomorrow’s stops and routes with the optimizer. Finally, act through a Databricks App, with Lakebase for audited writes and Genie for governed questions. The important part is the flow: fragmented feeds become trusted data, calendar rules become forecasts, manual routes become explainable plans, and radio knowledge becomes an auditable override.

title: What I'll show you
notes: Here’s what I’m going to show. Overview gives us current cash and risk. Route Tracking compares the fixed cycle with the optimized plan. Machines gives us a live ATM forecast. Truck Detail shows how a dispatcher changes the plan without losing the audit trail. If we have a minute, I’ll ask one plain-language question. For each step, I’ll tell you what to watch, show it, then bring it back to the decision you need to make.

title: Backup: plan vs today
notes: The live app isn’t responding, so I’ll switch to the captured view and keep us moving. The fixed cycle shows 135 stops, 1,711 kilometres, sixty-four machines at risk, and fourteen point seven percent inside opening hours. The optimized plan shows 97 stops, 1,323 kilometres, zero at risk, and 100 percent inside opening hours. CIT cost moves from 75,400 to 69,550 baht a day. The result is still synthetic, so the pilot tests whether it holds on your feeds.

title: Backup: forecast, override, ask
notes: This capture shows the three controls I wanted you to see. The forecast gives us a P50 to P80 range from live Model Serving, with about 81 percent P80 coverage. The override saves a skipped stop and its reason in Lakebase, so we know who changed what and why. Ask Cash Ops finds 79 critical nodes over the next three days. The app is the decision surface; the governed data and audit trail still sit underneath.

title: The outcome
notes: Let me bring that together. On this synthetic day, CIT cost falls eight percent, from 75,400 to 69,550 baht a day — about 1.5 million baht a year. Distance falls 23 percent, from 1,711 to 1,323 kilometres. Cash-out risk goes from 64 to zero. SLA moves from fourteen point seven percent to 100 percent, and 43 million baht of idle cash is released. Alex, that’s lower cost and risk. Shreya, it’s one governed path from feed to action.

title: Production readiness
notes: Let’s separate what’s ready from what needs work. The pipeline, job, and app are code in one Databricks Asset Bundle. It’s serverless, the app uses a scoped service principal, quality expectations are defined, the model has a champion alias in Unity Catalog, and Lakebase audits writes. Pilot gaps are IdP group mapping, maker-checker, dev and prod CI/CD, drift monitoring, and road-network travel times. The full job hasn’t run end to end on real feeds. The path is Khon Kaen Central, all three centres, then harden and extend.

title: Delivery risks and how we handle them
notes: Let’s talk about likely blockers. If the ATM switch sits behind a firewall, we’ll start safely with file drops into a Unity Catalog volume, then move to PrivateLink with both network teams. If timing slips, we’ll cut to one depot and file feeds, keep the success criteria, and re-plan with Alex. For PDPA, data stays in your workspace and region, PII is masked, and system tables provide audit evidence. I won’t quote commercials here; the account executive owns them. Which blocker feels most real? (pause)

title: The ask and next steps
notes: Let me close with a clear ask. Alex, this is a low-risk way to reduce CIT movement and idle cash without trading away customer trust. Shreya, it’s a governed design with honest gaps. I’m asking for a 30-day Khon Kaen Central pilot: at least 20 percent lower CIT cost or kilometres, cash-outs no higher, and at least 80 percent dispatcher acceptance. Alex sponsors the scoping session. Shreya brings Security and networking. I’ll bring the account team and our specialist. What would you need to see to sponsor that next step? (pause)

title: Appendix: decisions and trade-offs
notes: Here are the trade-offs we made. P80 lowers cash-out risk, but it can carry more cash. Thirteen vans meet every opening window, while thirty-eight unnecessary stops disappear and total cost still falls. A shared model is easier to govern, but we still need to test local payday behaviour. The optimizer is explainable and constrained, but road-network travel times must replace today’s straight-line-times-1.3 assumption. These are questions for the pilot, not hidden production claims.

title: Appendix: under the hood
notes: Shreya, here’s what sits underneath. Pipeline expectations reject bad records before planning. Custodian names and phone numbers are masked. Depot access is row-filtered, and lineage follows the data into the app. The forecast model is registered with a champion alias and served through a managed endpoint. The Asset Bundle keeps the pipeline, job, and app together. In the pilot, we’ll map those controls to your identity groups, add maker-checker and drift monitoring, and align deployment with your release process.
